newsitem.title: USA: UNDER PRESSURE, READER'S DIGEST CHANGES HELM.
newsitem.headline: UNDER PRESSURE, READER'S DIGEST CHANGES HELM.

text.p: The resignation of Reader's Digest Association Inc Chief Executive Officer James Schadt comes as the board was facing increasing pressure from Wall Street, unhappy with the sagging stock price, and lagging profits that showed no signs of improving anytime soon, analysts said.

The board was "facing a loss of confidence within the analyst community," said Linda Bannister, an analyst at Edwards Jones. "Maybe this was a move to get someone in with a different background, with new ideas."
"(Institutions) were dissatisfied," and that was recently conveyed to the board, said Karen Ficker at Furman Selz.
Investors appeared to applaud the resignation, sending the stock jumping 3-1/4 to 28-1/8 at midday.
The company has said a turnaround of the company would take more time. "It wasn't a matter of months but years," said Ficker. "You found a sense of frustration in the shareholder base..."
"There was a sense that time was running out" for Schadt, said Ficker.
Reader's Digest said George Grune, who served as CEO from 1984 to 1994, was named interim chairman and CEO, effective immediately.

Last month, the company cut the quarterly dividend in half and warned that earnings would be hurt by a fourth quarter charge of about $0.45 per share for inventory writedowns and a plan to improve its strategic growth. In April, it announced a $400 million program to boost business.
Among its key problems was revenue "softness" in the sales of books and home entertainment, such as video, which had represented 60 percent of total revenue, analysts said.
"It's really the most profitable piece of the business," Ficker said. "Although the magazine is the best known piece, it's just the front door of the company."
Analysts said the core problems were growing revenues and increasing the number of subscribers.

One analyst, who declined to be identified, said Schadt had a plan in place that was "intellectually very sound, but he didn't have evidence of a near-term turnaround, a quick fix," that could boost the depressed stock price. The stock has sunk steadily from about $50 in December 1995, and $40 at the start of 1997, to the mid $20s for much of this year.
Analysts agreed that the company still derives benefits from a strong brand name.
Schadt had told analysts in 1995 that any turnaround would take at least two years. But, Ficker said, the turnaround "was not happening at the pace we anticipated."
"People were not able to deal with a long-term turnaround, and wanted things to change quickly," said one analyst who declined to be identified.
A company spokeswoman said only that Schadt resigned to pursue personal interests. She declined to say whether the board asked him to resign.
